person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: Our central message is that social behavior can be triggered automatically by features of the environment.

span.label: automatic social behavior priming
span.quote: We propose that social behavior is often triggered automatically on the mere presence of relevant situational features; this behavior is unmediated by conscious perceptual or judgmental processes.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: The three experiments we report in this article were designed to provide a definitive test of this hypothesis.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: automatic behavior priming (perception-behavior link): activating a trait or stereotype concept directly and unconsciously increases the tendency to act in line with it
span.quote: participants for whom an elderly stereotype was primed walked more slowly down the hallway when leaving the experiment than did control participants, consistent with the content of that stereotype

span.label: The paper describes itself as a first demonstration whose boundary conditions are not yet known.
span.quote: As a first demonstration of automatic social behavior, the limits and parameters of these effects remain to be established.

span.label: The Experiment 1 timing measure suffered from a severe ceiling effect because most participants never interrupted.
span.quote: Fully 21 of the 34 participants did not interrupt at all in the 10 min available to them, so that the time variable suffered from a severe ceiling effect.

span.label: The authors concede the strength of behavioural versus judgemental priming effects cannot really be compared across their situations.
span.quote: Although ultimately one cannot really compare the strength of priming effects on behavioral versus judgmental measures, because there are too many differences between the experimental situations to allow for a meaningful comparison, we can point to some differences that are likely to produce greater or lesser priming effects.

span.label: the priming condition was assigned by a SECOND EXPERIMENTER who had no contact with the participant
span.note: eliminates: that the experimenter who ran the session knew the condition and shaped the behaviour being measured - the classic experimenter-expectancy route to a priming effect
span.quote: Which of the three versions (rude, polite, or neutral priming) the participant received had been randomly determined by another experimenter who did not have any contact with the participant, with the constraint that approximately equal numbers of participants received each of the forms.

span.label: participants were partially debriefed and questioned about whether they thought the scrambled-sentence task had influenced them
span.note: eliminates: that participants worked out the manipulation and complied with what they took to be the hypothesis
span.quote: After the participant had completed this task, he or she was partially debriefed and questioned concerning how they thought the first, scrambled-sentence test might have influenced them in the rest of the experiment.

span.label: priming
span.quote: Priming refers to the incidental activation of knowledge structures, such as trait concepts and stereotypes, by the current situational context

span.label: trait construct
span.quote: Across three experiments, the activation of a trait construct or a stereotype in one context resulted in behavior consistent with it in a subsequent unrelated context

span.label: stereotype
span.quote: Across three experiments, the activation of a trait construct or a stereotype in one context resulted in behavior consistent with it in a subsequent unrelated context

span.label: behavior
span.quote: Across three experiments, the activation of a trait construct or a stereotype in one context resulted in behavior consistent with it in a subsequent unrelated context

span.label: PRIMING DEFINED AS AN ORDINARY FEATURE OF BEING SOMEWHERE: `Priming refers to the INCIDENTAL ACTIVATION of knowledge structures, such as trait concepts and stereotypes, BY THE CURRENT SITUATIONAL CONTEXT.` **Not a laboratory operation - a description of what situations do to people continuously**, of which the experiment is a controlled instance. That is the same move srull-wyer1979 makes when it says accessibility rises with the number of activations `IN THE PAST`, and it is what licenses generalising from a word-scramble task to walking down a corridor
span.quote: Priming refers to the incidental activation of knowledge structures, such as trait concepts and stereotypes, by the current situational context

span.label: THE DESIGN LOGIC IN ONE SENTENCE: `The same priming techniques that have been shown in prior research to influence IMPRESSION FORMATION produce similar effects when THE DEPENDENT MEASURE IS SWITCHED to social behavior.` **Only the dependent measure changed.** The manipulation is held constant against the 1977-79 accessibility work and the outcome is swapped from a judgement to an action - which makes this a claim about the SCOPE of an established effect rather than a new effect. **And it means the replication debate about this paper is unavoidably also about higgins1977 and srull-wyer1979**, both of which are in this corpus
span.quote: The same priming techniques that have been shown in prior research to influence impression formation produce similar effects when the dependent measure is switched to social behavior

span.label: THE EFFECT TAKES THE CONTENT OF WHAT WAS PRIMED, WHICH IS WHAT RULES OUT AROUSAL OR MOOD: rudeness produced interrupting `more quickly and frequently`, the elderly stereotype produced walking `more slowly down the hallway ... CONSISTENT WITH THE CONTENT OF THAT STEREOTYPE`, and the third prime produced hostility. **Three primes, three different behaviours, each matching its own prime** - a general activation account predicts one direction for all three and gets none of them
span.quote: In Experiment 2, participants for whom an elderly stereotype was primed walked more slowly down the hallway when leaving the experiment than did control participants, consistent with the content of that stereotype

span.label: AND TWO THEORETICAL PERSPECTIVES ARE OFFERED WITH NEITHER CHOSEN. First, situationally linked behaviour: `a person has behavioral responses (e.g., assertiveness, anger, patience) that are ASSOCIATIVELY LINKED TO PARTICULAR SITUATIONS.` Then: `another theoretical perspective CONSISTENT WITH the present findings is that of an AUTOMATIC PERCEPTION-BEHAVIOR LINK.` **Both are said to fit and the paper stops there.** dijksterhuis1998, tagged one record earlier, takes the second and builds on it - so the corpus holds the fork and the branch that was taken
span.quote: One explanation for the present results is in terms of situationally linked behavior; that is, that a person has behavioral responses (e.g., assertiveness, anger, patience) that are associatively linked to particular situations

span.label: extends → priming research on social perception
span.quote: We argue here that such passive, automatic effects of priming need not be limited to social perception.

span.label: extends → Berkowitz and LePage (1967) and Carver et al. (1983)
span.quote: These studies showed that the intentional behavior could be affected in intensity or duration by the aggression priming manipulation (the presence of guns or prior exposure to synonyms of aggression), but they did not show the behavior to be produced automatically, in the absence of that explicitly given intention.

span.label: builds-on → Carver et al. (1983) behavioral schema model
span.quote: Thus, our results are in harmony with those of Carver et al. (1983), who advanced a "behavioral schema" model as an explanation for modeling effects.

span.label: replicates → Devine (1989, Experiment 2)
span.quote: This finding corresponds to that of Devine (1989, Experiment 2), who found that the automatic effect of the African American stereotype on social perception did not vary as a function of level of consciously expressed prejudice, as measured by the Modern Racism Scale.

span.label: trait construct —causes→ behavior
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.9 — **`CONSISTENT WITH IT` AND `SUBSEQUENT UNRELATED CONTEXT` ARE BOTH IN THE QUOTE AND BOTH ARE LOAD-BEARING.** The behaviour matches the CONTENT of what was primed, which excludes a general arousal account; and the second context is UNRELATED, which is what makes it a carry-over rather than a demand effect. Weight 0.9: the discussion's opening summary of three experiments, and this is the paper's central claim.
span.quote: Across three experiments, the activation of a trait construct or a stereotype in one context resulted in behavior consistent with it in a subsequent unrelated context

span.label: stereotype —causes→ behavior
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.9 — **`increases` MEANS MORE STEREOTYPE-CONSISTENT BEHAVIOUR, NOT MORE OF ANY MEASURED QUANTITY, AND THE DISTINCTION MATTERS HERE.** In Experiment 2 the measurement WENT DOWN - participants primed with `elderly` WALKED MORE SLOWLY. A reader taking `increases` as `the number went up` would have that experiment backwards. The axis is recording consistency with the primed content, which is what the quote says, and the three experiments move three different dependent variables in three directions.
span.quote: Across three experiments, the activation of a trait construct or a stereotype in one context resulted in behavior consistent with it in a subsequent unrelated context
